title: Where a Virtual Service Edge runs and which platforms can cluster

prose.label: Which platforms can cluster.
prose.text: {{cluster-mode-selectable-on-esxi}} {{public-cloud-no-native-cluster}} Hyper-V is where the documentation disagrees with itself ([[zia.virtual-service-edge.platforms:hyper-v-cluster-mode]]); treat ESXi as the only platform with an unambiguous native cluster. The cluster mechanics for that case are [[zia.virtual-service-edge.clusters]] and [[zia.virtual-service-edge.load-balancing]].

prose.label: The comparison with the hardware form factor.

prose.text: The public cloud pages are in [[zia.virtual-service-edge.cloud-deployment]] and the VM install sequence is in [[zia.virtual-service-edge.bring-up]].

One more disagreement to know about: the minimum ESXi version differs between the specifications table and the cluster configuration article ([[zia.virtual-service-edge.platforms:esxi-minimum-version]]).

checks.do: Which platform the deployment runs on, since only VMware ESXi offers Cluster as a deployment mode.

comparison-vse.statement: In the Private versus Virtual Service Edge comparison, the Virtual Service Edge is easy to deploy and can handle remote user traffic; it can be deployed flexibly in the DMZ, the internal network or the public cloud, is horizontally scalable, needs no wait for shipping and no public IPs, and has a built-in load balancer. The organization is responsible for deployment, configuration and maintenance, though upgrades are automatic, and it provides the hardware and hypervisor while Zscaler provides the host software. An SSL acceleration card is recommended for deployments requiring a throughput of 100 Mbps or more to perform SSL inspection, and the page says Virtual Service Edges must be deployed either in clusters or standalone for production.

quotes: Easy to deploy. Can handle remote user traffic.

Flexible deployment in the DMZ, your internal network, or in the public cloud. Virtual form factor that is horizontally scalable. Instantly available, with no need to wait for shipping. No need to use or purchase public IPs. Built-in load balancer.
You are responsible for the deployment, configuration, and maintenance. However, upgrades are automatic.
You provide the hardware and hypervisor, while Zscaler provides the Zscaler host software that runs on the VMs.
An SSL acceleration card is recommended for deployments requiring a throughput of 100 Mbps or more in order to perform SSL inspection on Virtual Service Edges.
You must deploy them either in clusters or standalone for production.

hyper-v.statement: The Hyper-V page says Zscaler supports a standalone Virtual Service Edge for production deployments on Microsoft Hyper-V. It lists Windows Server 2019 with the Hyper-V feature enabled, a minimum of 48 GB RAM and 3 network interfaces (1 for management, 1 for the Virtual Service Edge and 1 for the Load Balancer), and a Generation 1 VM. Promiscuous Mode must be enabled using the Microsoft NDIS capture on the virtual switch, because Zscaler load balancers and Virtual Service Edges use CARP, and the commands must be run as an administrator. MAC address spoofing on the third NIC facilitates sending of frames by the Virtual/Cluster IP, and Zscaler recommends different servers for each instance to achieve fault tolerance.

quotes: Zscaler supports standalone Virtual Service Edge for Internet & SaaS (ZIA) for production deployments on Microsoft Hyper-V.
Hypervisor: Windows Server 2019 with Hyper-V feature enabled
The Promiscuous Mode option must be enabled using the Microsoft NDIS capture on the Virtual Switch.
Zscaler load balancers and Virtual Service Edges use the Common Address Redundancy Protocol (CARP) to process traffic across multiple Virtual Service Edge instances.
In order to support this, enabling promiscuous mode on your Windows Server is required.
You must run these commands as an administrator.
Minimum Required RAM: 48 GB
Network Interfaces: 3 interfaces (1 for Management, 1 for the Virtual Service Edge, and 1 for the Load Balancer).
On the Specify Generation screen, select Generation 1 and click Next.
The third NIC in the Virtual Service Edge has CARP enabled by the Load Balancer. So, enabling the MAC address spoofing facilitates sending of frames by the Virtual/Cluster IP.
Zscaler recommends using different servers for each instance to achieve fault tolerance.

nutanix-modes.statement: The Nutanix page says Virtual Service Edges can be deployed in a cluster or in standalone mode with Nutanix, and Zscaler recommends clusters to achieve redundancy and update software seamlessly during scheduled update cycles. A cluster can contain a maximum of 16 instances, each needing a subscription license count, and the hypervisor is Nutanix AHV (AOS 6.x and later; verified on AOS 7.3).

quotes: You can deploy Virtual Service Edges for Internet & SaaS (ZIA) in a cluster or in standalone mode with Nutanix.
Zscaler recommends deploying Virtual Service Edges in clusters to achieve redundancy and update software seamlessly during scheduled update cycles.
It can contain a maximum of 16 Virtual Service Edge instances. You need a subscription license count for each Virtual Service Edge in a cluster.
Hypervisor: Nutanix AHV (AOS 6.x and later; verified on AOS 7.3).

nutanix-carp-network.statement: On Nutanix AHV no equivalent of the promiscuous mode toggle is needed, and CARP advertisements (multicast 224.0.0.18) reach every instance automatically. Where anti-spoofing is enforced (for example a Nutanix Flow microsegmentation policy), MAC spoofing on the vNICs must be explicitly allowed and CARP/VRRP multicast permitted. The page lists a dedicated AHV network on its own VLAN, a standard NIC in Access mode (kNormalNic) rather than kDirectNic or SR-IOV, IGMP snooping left disabled because enabling it can prune CARP multicast and HA might fail, and an uplink bond of active-backup or LACP with balance-tcp, not balance-slb.

quotes: Promiscuous Mode: No equivalent toggle is needed on AHV.
so CARP advertisements (multicast 224.0.0.18) reach every Public Service Edge instance automatically.

If anti-spoofing is enforced (for example, a Nutanix Flow microsegmentation policy or a hardened network profile), you must explicitly allow MAC spoofing on the Virtual Service Edge vNICs and permit CARP/VRRP multicast in that policy.
Dedicated network: Create and use a dedicated AHV network (using its own VLAN) for Virtual Service Edge interfaces instead of sharing the VLAN with general corporate VMs.

NIC type: Use a standard NIC in Access mode (type kNormalNic). Do not use a Direct-mode NIC (kDirectNic) or SR-IOV because these bypass the OVS bridge chain and are only for cases explicitly directed by Nutanix Support.
IGMP snooping: Leave disabled (the AHV default) on the virtual switch carrying Virtual Service Edge traffic. If enabled, CARP multicast can be pruned and HA might fail.

Uplink bond mode: Use active-backup (the AHV default) or LACP with balance-tcp. Do not use the balance-slb bond mode, which drops multicast and broadcast on non-active secondaries and causes CARP not to function properly.

nutanix-vm.statement: The Nutanix VM image is created with image type DISK, 4 vCPUs, 48 GB memory, Legacy BIOS boot and a SCSI bus disk of 500 GB (thin provisioned), for which Zscaler recommends SSDs.

quotes: Image Type: Select DISK.
vCPU(s): Enter 4.
Memory: Enter 48.
Minimum Required RAM: 48 GB for standalone and nodes of a cluster.
Boot Configuration: Select Legacy BIOS.
Bus Type: Select SCSI.
Disk: 500 GB (thin provisioned). Zscaler recommends using SSDs.

full-featured-dedicated.statement: A Virtual Service Edge uses a VM to function as a full-featured Public Service Edge dedicated to the organization's traffic, performing the same service as the Public Service Edges in the Zscaler cloud, including Firewall, Sandbox and DLP.

quotes: Virtual Service Edges use a VM to function as a full-featured Public Service Edge dedicated to your organization
Virtual Service Edges perform the same service as the Public Service Edges in the Zscaler cloud, including support for features, such as Firewall, Sandbox, and Data Loss Prevention (DLP).

approval-and-licence.statement: Zscaler typically recommends forwarding traffic to the Public Service Edges. An organization with different traffic-flow needs can extend the Zscaler architecture to its premises by licensing and deploying Virtual Service Edges, with Zscaler's approval.

quotes: Zscaler typically recommends that organizations forward traffic to the Public Service Edges for Internet & SaaS in the Zscaler cloud.
then with Zscaler's approval, you can extend the Zscaler patented cloud architecture to your organization's premises by licensing and deploying Virtual Service Edges.

reasons-to-deploy.statement: The documented reasons are locations with geopolitical requirements and regulations, high latency to a Public Service Edge, applications that require the organization's IP address as the source IP address, and users who need localized content.

quotes: Locations with certain geopolitical requirements and regulations.
Locations that experience high latency when connecting to a Public Service Edge.
Applications that require an organization's IP address as the source IP address.
Users who need to see localized content.

supported-platforms.statement: Virtual Service Edges are supported on VMware ESX/ESXi, Microsoft Azure, AWS EC2, Microsoft Hyper-V and Google Cloud Platform.

quotes: Virtual Service Edges are supported on VMware ESX/ESXi, Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2, Microsoft Hyper-V, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP).

image-downloads.statement: The Virtual Service Edges page offers downloads of the Virtual Service Edge VM, the SNMP MIB files, the Hyper-V VM and the Nutanix VM.

quotes: Download a Virtual Service Edge VM.
Download the SNMP MIB files.
Download the Hyper-V VM.
Download the Nutanix VM.

os-24-or-later.statement: A new or clean Virtual Service Edge deployment requires a VM image running Zscaler OS version 24 or later.

quotes: New or clean deployment of Virtual Service Edge requires a virtual machine (VM) image running on Zscaler OS version 24 or later.

vmotion-esxi-7.statement: vMotion is supported only on VMware ESXi 7.0 and above.

quotes: | vMotion Support | VMware ESXi 7.0 and above | - | - | - | - |

cluster-mode-selectable-on-esxi.statement: When adding a Virtual Service Edge the Deployment Mode can be Cluster or Standalone only on VMware ESXi; on other platforms only Standalone is selectable. The SDK's field documentation says the same.

quotes: Deployment Mode: Select either Cluster or Standalone if you have the VMware ESXi platform. Otherwise, select only Standalone.
Select either STANDALONE or CLUSTER if you have the VMware ESXi platform. Otherwise, select only STANDALONE.

public-cloud-no-native-cluster.statement: In public cloud environments the native cluster mode of deployment is not supported, and public cloud load balancers provide redundancy between Virtual Service Edges. The page lists Microsoft Azure, AWS EC2, Microsoft Hyper-V and GCP in that sentence.

quotes: In public cloud environments such as Microsoft Azure, AWS EC2, Microsoft Hyper-V, and GCP, the native cluster mode of deployment is not supported, and you can use public cloud load balancers to ensure redundancy between the Virtual Service Edges.

nutanix-release-entry.statement: The ZIA release summary entry dated July 13, 2026 lists Virtual Service Edge configuration as supported on the Nutanix platform, with the Nutanix VM image downloadable on the Virtual Service Edges page.

quotes: Virtual Service Edge configuration is supported on the Nutanix platform.
You can download the Nutanix VM image on the Virtual Service Edges page.

hyper-v-memory.summary: The memory the Hyper-V page requires for a Virtual Service Edge VM.

quotes: Minimum Required RAM: 48 GB

positions.says: The requirements list gives a minimum of 48 GB RAM.

quotes: On the Assign Memory screen, set the Startup memory to 32768 MB and click Next.

positions.says: The VM-creation step sets the startup memory to 32768 MB.

hyper-v-memory.impact: A VM built by following the creation step has less memory than the listed minimum; the page does not say whether the memory is raised later.

hyper-v-cluster-mode.summary: Whether Microsoft Hyper-V supports the native Virtual Service Edge cluster mode.

quotes: Zscaler load balancers and Virtual Service Edges use the Common Address Redundancy Protocol (CARP) to process traffic across multiple Virtual Service Edge instances.
The third NIC in the Virtual Service Edge has CARP enabled by the Load Balancer. So, enabling the MAC address spoofing facilitates sending of frames by the Virtual/Cluster IP.

positions.says: The Hyper-V configuration page builds a CARP cluster, with the load balancer enabling CARP on the third NIC and MAC spoofing allowing the virtual or cluster IP to send frames.

quotes: | Maximum VMs per Cluster | 16 | - | - | 16 | - |
In the VMware ESXi and Microsoft Hyper-V environments, Zscaler recommends utilizing the in-built load balancer for Virtual Service Edges deployed in cluster mode.

positions.says: Hyper-V has a maximum of 16 VMs per cluster and uses the in-built load balancer in cluster mode.

quotes: In public cloud environments such as Microsoft Azure, AWS EC2, Microsoft Hyper-V, and GCP, the native cluster mode of deployment is not supported

positions.says: Hyper-V is listed with Azure, AWS and GCP as an environment where native cluster mode is not supported.

quotes: Deployment Mode: Select either Cluster or Standalone if you have the VMware ESXi platform. Otherwise, select only Standalone.

positions.says: Only VMware ESXi can select the Cluster deployment mode; every other platform, Hyper-V included, selects Standalone.

hyper-v-cluster-mode.impact: A Hyper-V cluster design cannot be assumed to work from the documentation. Two statements and the SDK's field documentation point to ESXi as the only clustering platform; the sizing table and one recommendation say Hyper-V clusters. Confirm with Zscaler before planning one.

quotes: | Hypervisor Support | VMware ESXi 6.0 and later | Microsoft Azure | AWS EC2 | Microsoft Hyper-V | GCP |
Hypervisor: VMware ESX/ESXi v5.0 and later.

positions.says: VMware ESX/ESXi v5.0 and later for a Virtual Service Edge cluster.

esxi-minimum-version.impact: Low for new builds, which will be on a current ESXi release, but a legacy host on ESXi 5.x is documented as supported in one place and not the other.

nutanix-support-scope.title: What Nutanix support establishes
nutanix-support-scope.detail: The Nutanix configuration page now states cluster and standalone modes, a 16-instance cluster maximum and the AHV and AOS versions (nutanix-modes); throughput, SSL card support and whether the public-cloud load-balancer model applies are not stated. Unverified legacy statement: that the Nutanix release 'does not establish Nutanix cluster topology, sizing, or parity with the existing platform table.' Whether Nutanix supports native clustering, the bundled load balancer, a cluster size, or the public-cloud load-balancer model is not stated.
